Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,
a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed
$200 million
to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

Our mission
We build the foundation for understanding AI’s economic impact. The Anthropic Economic Index tracks how AI tools are being used around the world and across every sector of the economy. Alongside regular Economic Index reports, we produce novel research that studies the economic implications of AI, and fund ambitious external research.
Producing reliable data to guide policy
The speed of AI development means the stakes are unusually high. We need reliable data to inform the decisions that workers, employers, and policymakers make about the future. Our research provides evidence to address uncertainty and help society navigate this transition.

NVIDIA CUDA Tile
(cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model that abstracts thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives to automatically target Tensor Cores and other advanced GPU hardware features.
Machine learning engineers at
Jane Street
implemented the Mamba-2 state-space model in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize three custom kernels for the forward pass: chunk_cumsum, fwd_pass_state, and compute_out.
The chunk_cumsum kernel computes per-token, per-head cumulative sums of the decay term in log-space using ct.cumsum, storing results for reuse by the subsequent kernels.
The fwd_pass_state kernel uses ct.mma to execute Tensor Core matrix-multiply operations that advance the hidden state across sequence chunks, applying the jump formula with exponential decay and pre-multiplied operands.
The compute_out kernel fuses the carried-state term, the decayed and causally masked interaction matrix, and the skip connection into a single tiled kernel that keeps intermediate matrices in registers and casts to TF32 for Tensor Core execution.
Performance optimizations include latency hints for DRAM traffic modeling, operand swapping to route fused operands to Tensor Memory, transposed memory layouts for TMA-friendly access, and an autotuner that searches block size and occupancy parameters for each input shape.

NVIDIA CUDA Tile
(cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores.
As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at
Jane Street
implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them.
Overview and prerequisites
To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the
cuTile Python Quickstart
guide. Import the package as
cuda.tile
and expose it as
ct
throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post.
Sequence modeling computational trade-off
Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length.
Mamba-2 architecture
The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores.
The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is:
\(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\)
y
t
=
c
t
⊤
h

D

y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t
Where:
\(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\)
\(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\)
\(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity)
\(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters
Intuitively:
\(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\)
\(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention
\(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention
\(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention
The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size
S,H
(\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply:
\(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\)
This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores.
An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just:
\(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\)
If building a matrix \(B\) of shape (
T, S
) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape (
T, H
) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\):
Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events
With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given
only
\(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula.
Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute:
\(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\)
Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this:
Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states
Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention).
When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection):
\(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
With \(M\) the traditional causal mask.
Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation
Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like:
\(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\)
Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation:
\(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\)
Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following:
\(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability.
Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe
This will translate into three kernels:
chunk_cumsum
: Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk.
fwd_pass_state
: Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above.
compute_out
: Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step.
Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums
The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk.
The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay
a
and a per-token timestep
dt
. The effective decay at token
t
for head
h
is
a[h] * dt[t, h]
, and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute
exp2
instead of
exp
, the result is scaled by
log2(e)
.
This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use:
ct.bid
,
ct.load
/
ct.store
, and
ct.cumsum
.
The full kernel is short:
@ct.kernel
def chunk_cumsum_kernel(
a: torch.Tensor,        # [num_heads]
dt: torch.Tensor,       # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
output: torch.Tensor,   # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
chunk_size: ct.Constant[int],
BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int],
) -> None:
chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2)
dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx),
shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H),
padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,),
shape=(BLOCK_H,),
padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E
ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype))

(num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size)
, the first line determines where you are in the grid using
ct.bid

a_tile
(shape
[BLOCK_H]
) and
dt_tile
(shape
[1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H]
) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile.
ct.cumsum(..., axis=1)
then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by
fwd_pass_state
and
compute_out
.
Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state

computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that

[BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE]

AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have gone from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. As a result, the current workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM.
NVIDIA RTX Spark
is built for AI development. Thanks to the NVIDIA GB10 system-on-a-chip and large unified memory, developers can run local coding agents, access AI frameworks, and code, test, and deploy on a single PC.
One machine to code, test, and deploy
RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops enable developers to complete all of their workflow on a single machine.
Developers can choose to work in Windows, including the new Windows Developer Config, developed with Microsoft, which installs the top development frameworks, mutes notifications, enhances the terminal, and can move their task bar to the side. Or they can work in Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they get access to the same environment and dependencies they will use when deploying to the cloud.
This enables developers to complete all their work in their target OS without code migrations. And since RTX Spark has an NVIDIA GPU, developers can test and deploy to the largest local AI installed base: 150 million RTX PCs, as well as virtually all the clouds in the world that run on NVIDIA GPUs.
With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI compute, developers can run coding models locally, including Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, reducing cloud coding agent token consumption.
The performance you need for AI development
Development has gone from being a CPU-bound workload, where performance was determined mostly by the CPU, to a GPU-bound workload. AI developers today need to run inference to run their coding agents and test their apps; for fine-tuning and training models; and yes, still a bit of compilation.
Thanks to the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU in RTX Spark, these laptops and desktops come equipped with all the compute required for inference, fine-tuning and compilation. Compared with Intel’s Panther Lake 12Xe, RTX Spark delivers 4.6x performance on coding agents, 2.7x performance on fine-tuning, and 1.8x performance on code compilation.
Figure 1. NVIDIA developer-workload comparison, with Intel Core Ultra X9 388H normalized to 1.0. Tests: AA-AgentPerf-local with Qwen3.8-27B; Unsloth LoRA with Llama-3.1-8B; and Linux kernel compilation using Phoronix Test Suite
A familiar software stack, expanded for Windows
NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to advance the Windows on Arm developer landscape. Together with RTX Spark, the community is releasing multiple new tools, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build, the first Python release that is native by default with Python 3.15, over 2,000 ready-to-use Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages.
A key advantage of developing on NVIDIA hardware is access to the largest ecosystem of developer tools, from coding agents, to AI models, to frameworks.
Because NVIDIA GPUs are the most widely used platform for AI development, new tools and frameworks typically work on NVIDIA from day one, while support for other hardware follows weeks later. There’s also access to NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including tools such as FlashInfer for LLM acceleration and NVIDIA NeMo libraries tools for AI model development.
NVIDIA also provides a repository of
NVIDIA Skills
that teach agents how to use CUDA-X libraries, enabling developers to build GPU-accelerated applications without requiring deep familiarity with CUDA.
Figure 2. RTX Spark’s ecosystem of agents, models, frameworks, and CUDA-X libraries
Local coding agents come to RTX Spark
RTX Spark devices are ideal for local coding agents. NVIDIA has collaborated closely with the top agents, including GitHub Copilot, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw, to improve them and make them easier to use.
The improvements include:
Seamless deployment of local models with optimized recipes
Enhanced security with NVIDIA OpenShell and/or Microsoft Execution Containers, delivering OS-level sandboxing
Hybrid prompt routers between local and cloud models, so that prompts get sent to local models if they are good enough, or escalated to cloud if needed, reducing token consumption
Microsoft GitHub CoPilot now enables seamless local AI through Windows ML, which is now supported with llama.cpp as a backend. The prompt router HydraFusion has been upgraded to also support local models. And the new MAI 1.1 Coding Flash model can run locally on RTX Spark.
Pi
, an open-source coding agent with a lightweight terminal interface and support for local and cloud models, is also optimized for RTX Spark. Its extensions, skills, and prompt templates give developers control over how the agent fits into their workflow, from model selection to the tools it can use.
JetBrains has launched native support for
Junie Local on RTX Spark
. The coding agent reads code, edits files, and runs tests, with the model and code staying on the machine. Junie Local sizes its context window to the memory available to the GPU, so RTX Spark unified memory lets it keep more code, tool output, and conversation history in context.
New Nemotron models offer more options for local agents
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark.
This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.
Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.
Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.
Decision models now supported in top frameworks
Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests, to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in
llama.cpp
and
Unsloth
on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs.
AI for media SDKs
The
NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs
are now available for RTX Spark, including Python wheel with support for video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR. The wheel is available on PyPI, with C++ SDKs also available on NGC for RTX Spark and Windows on Arm.
Bring your Windows applications to RTX Spark
To bring an existing application to RTX Spark, first assess dependencies for Windows on Arm. Choose a native Arm64 build or use Arm64EC to migrate components incrementally. Test installation, functionality, performance, and the NVIDIA and CUDA paths your app uses.
NVIDIA’s app-porting resources
explain the migration options and tools, including how to start preparation on an existing Windows on Arm development system.
Find your RTX Spark and start building
RTX Spark is available now in laptops, and coming in November to small form factor desktops that are ideal for always on, 24×7 running agents.
Explore RTX Spark systems
to find your favorite and see available purchasing options.
Once you get your own, get started with the
AI Development playbook
to configure Windows, set up your agent, and connect NVIDIA Skills. And learn about how you can get started
developing Local AI apps
for NVIDIA GPUs.

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RIS
items.content:
Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
- Google Developers Blog
Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
OCT. 20, 2026
Billy Rutledge
Eng Director
Google Research
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Some of the most compelling use cases for AI are happening directly on the devices around us. You see it first in personal devices like wearables that need to understand context in real time, and increasingly in enterprise and industrial systems like autonomous robots and smart sensors. These experiences require low latency, strict privacy, and all-day reliability that cannot depend on a constant round-trip to the cloud.
Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.
Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.
Last year, Google Research
introduced Coral NPU
with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.
Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:
The complete 32-bit Coral NPU architecture (Milestones 1–4):
Including our
new Matrix Execution Unit
, configurable for up to 1 TOPS and targeting 10mW average power for inference.
The Coral Compiler v1.0, based on IREE/MLIR:
An
open-source, end-to-end compiler
and simulation stack that takes JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow models straight to the Coral NPU hardware target.
New MCU chip with Coral NPU:
Unveiling the
2nd-gen Synaptics Astra® SR200 series
(400 GOPS) microcontroller chips.
New Coralboard kits:
Launching
the new Coralboard™ SR
, plus global availability of the Coralboard SL (1 TOPS) from
DigiKey
.
Co-designing silicon and software: The right performance at the right power envelope
Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.
We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.
Completing the Coral NPU 32-bit architecture
Over the past year,
we released the first three milestones
of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.
Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.
Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.
Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.
To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete
32-bit RTL
is available today on GitHub.
Bridging models to silicon with the v1.0 IREE/MLIR compiler
To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our
open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain
.
With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.
The ecosystem in action: From foundry and IP readiness to commercial silicon
Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with
VeriSilicon
on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with
GlobalFoundries
on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.
On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.
At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three
commercial silicon
and
hardware products
built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:
2nd-Gen Silicon — Synaptics Astra SR200 Series
: Taped out and launching this month, the
SR200
series integrates second-generation Coral NPU IP (including Milestone 2 RISC-V Vector Core support) to deliver 400 GOPS in an ultra-low-power MCU package. It is built for battery-powered wearables and industrial sensor nodes.
New Synaptics Coralboard SR Unveiled:
A new
Coralboard SR
developer kit powered by the Astra SR200 series, designed for rapid prototyping of MCU-class Edge and Physical AI applications.
Synaptics Coralboard SL Reaches General Availability (GA):
Following our limited-edition preview at Google I/O, the
Coralboard SL
is now generally available worldwide through
DigiKey
, with SDKs and documentation on the
Synaptics Coralboard Developer page
. Powered by the Astra SL2619 processor with a 1 TOPS Torq™ / Coral NPU subsystem, it brings transformer and multi-stream vision acceleration to Linux-based IoT and robotics.
Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner
Grinn
, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.
Start building with Coral NPU
With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.
Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:
Read the docs:
Visit
developers.google.com/coral
for architecture guides, documentation, and tutorials.
Explore the code:
Check out the complete
32-bit RTL
(including the Milestone 4 Matrix Execution Unit), the
v1.0 IREE/MLIR compiler
stack, and the
MPACT simulator
on
GitHub
.
Get a devkit:
Order the generally available
Synaptics Coralboard SL
today on
DigiKey
, and explore the new
Astra SR200
series and Coralboard SR on the
Synaptics Coralboard Developer page
.

items.content:
Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
- Google Developers Blog
Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
OCT. 20, 2026
Qi Zhou
Principal Software Engineer
Chris Chan
Group Product Manager
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
As part of our
broader announcements
for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).
Background
For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.
So we started in earnest on
TorchTPU
, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new
vLLM
and
SGLang
engines on top of it.
Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.
The Inference Stack
Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.
Engine Overview
TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a
tpu
device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via
torch.compile
using XLA, and collectives go through
torch.distributed
.
Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager and API server etc, and add TPU implementations underneath.
Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in vLLM or SGLang, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace
Workload support
Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.
Here’s the list of supported features:
Agentic & Multi-Turn:
Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
Interactive & Low Latency:
Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
High-throughput Batch:
Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
Long Context:
Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
Disaggregated Serving:
Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
Multimodal:
Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
Very Large Models:
Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints
Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.
Moving the KV Cache with TPU Sync
Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.
Both engines use
TPU Sync
for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.
Running today in production & public benchmarks
Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.
Building on our
initial submission
of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading
2.01 cents
. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new
state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX
, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.
Building with the community
We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:
SGLang-TorchTPU was
co-developed
with RadixArk (founded by the creators of SGLang)
This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.
"SGLang-TorchTPU is running in production at Meta today, and getting there was a close three-way collaboration between Meta, Google, and the SGLang team to make the stack production-ready. It gives us a remarkably mature, PyTorch-native serving stack that integrates effortlessly into our existing AI infrastructure, with the performance, reliability, and flexibility we need to run frontier workloads efficiently on TPUs. " said Zongwei Zhou, PyTorch-TPU lead at Meta.
"At RadixArk, TorchTPU has supercharged our development velocity as we roll out SGLang support across diverse silicon. It’s given us a painless path to native TPU acceleration, passing massive efficiency gains and flexible compute choices directly down to our customers," said Banghua Zhu, CTO and co-founder of RadixArk.
vLLM-TorchTPU was
co-developed
with Inferact (founded by the creators of vLLM)
Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas
megakernel
for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary
AgentX submission
for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.
"Our mission at Inferact has always been to make high-performance inference accessible, reliable, and cost-effective across the entire AI ecosystem. We are thrilled to partner on the launch of TorchTPU and bring first-class support for vLLM to TPUs. By bridging PyTorch’s optimized TPU capabilities directly into vLLM, developers can immediately run production workloads on TPUs with the high throughput, low latency, and memory efficiency they expect from our stack," said Simon Mo, CEO and co-founder of Inferact.
To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to both engines. Request
here
.
Roadmap
As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!
Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma4 and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.
A note on our JAX runtimes
vLLM-Jax
, and
SGLang-JAX
remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.
Getting started
Get started today:
vLLM-TorchTPU:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu
SGLang-TorchTPU:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu
TorchTPU:
https://github.com/google-pytorch/torch_tpu

Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
- Google Developers Blog
Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
OCT. 20, 2026
Eric Yang
Software Engineer
Alan Ma
Staff Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Model Explorer goes beyond high-level model graphs. See how Arm plugs in custom compiler IRs, verifies NPU delegation side-by-side, and maps cycle-level profiling traces directly onto your execution graph.
Machine learning models run locally on a wide range of hardware, from low-power edge devices to gaming graphics and physical AI systems. Running models efficiently on these targets requires compilation steps such as quantization, graph lowering, operator fusion, and hardware delegation.
Arm used
Google AI Edge Model Explorer
to give developers visibility into these pipelines. With Model Explorer's hierarchical graph visualization and plugin architecture, Arm built several open-source adapters that make edge model transformations easier to inspect.
The Challenge
When deploying a model to edge hardware, a framework change or operator constraint can alter the exported execution graph. Engineers often need to answer three questions:
Structural integrity:
Did graph lowering introduce unintended operators such as extra layout transposes?
Hardware delegation:
Is the model fully delegated to the NPU or GPU, or are unsupported subgraphs falling back to the CPU?
Cycle-level bottlenecks:
Which nodes in the lowered graph take the most compute cycles?
Answering these questions by reading raw flatbuffers or text logs takes time, especially for large language models (LLMs) and neural networks. Arm needed a visual tool to inspect Arm-specific intermediate representations and hardware profiling traces.
How Arm Used Model Explorer's Visual Debugging Workflows
To address these deployment challenges, Arm developed custom adapters for Google AI Edge Model Explorer to support several model formats (i.e.,
TOSA
,
VGF
, and
PTE
), establishing a comprehensive visual workflow for on-device optimization. Using these extensions, engineering teams can validate exported pipelines, verify accelerator delegation, and pinpoint cycle-level performance bottlenecks directly on the model graph:
1. Catching hidden export regressions in VGF
Arm engineers used Model Explorer to validate a PyTorch-trained
Neural Super Sampling (NSS) model
exported through the ExecuTorch Arm backend as a VGF file for Vulkan ML Extensions. While inspecting the VGF graph, the team found unintended
TRANSPOSE
operators introduced by a change in the ExecuTorch Arm backend.
Figure 1: Overview of the exported NSS model in VGF format, showing the graph partition and its connections to the model inputs and outputs.
Model Explorer enables users to inspect individual nodes of the model graph, such as the
rescale
operator depicted below, which displays the operator's attributes and SPIR-V tensor connections. This functionality assisted the Arm team in identifying and resolving the regression without requiring manual analysis of raw log files.
Figure 2: Detailed view of the NSS graph, showing a selected rescale operator with its attributes and SPIR-V input and output connections.
2. Verifying NPU delegation vs. CPU fallback with Split-Pane View
To optimize vision models for accelerators like the
Arm Ethos-U85 NPU
, Arm engineers used
Model Explorer's
split-pane view
to compare CPU and NPU-delegated graphs side-by-side for a Ultralytics YOLO model.
The split-pane view showed the structural difference: the CPU graph displays each individual layer, while the NPU graph groups the network into a single
EthosUBackend
block between
quantize
and
dequantize
nodes. For partially supported models in
LiteRT
or
ExecuTorch
, this view helps identify un-delegated operators and split subgraphs.
Figure 3a: Ultralytics YOLO model CPU graph in split-pane view
Figure 3b: Ultralytics YOLO model NPU graph in split-pane view
3. Pinpointing Hardware Bottlenecks with Per-node Trace Overlays
To find latency bottlenecks on the Ethos-U NPU, Arm ran their model on their
Fixed Virtual Platform (FVP)
simulator and used
Model Explorer's
node data plugin
to overlay cycle-accurate execution traces onto the graph. Color-coded heatmaps showed that a single
TRANSPOSE
node was the main latency bottleneck.
Figure 4. Highlighted performance data overlay that clearly shows where the bottleneck is.
How to get started
You can use Google AI Edge Model Explorer along with Arm's open-source adapters today to inspect and optimize your own on-device models locally via PyPI or GitHub.
Install Google AI Edge Model Explorer
Install adapter and launch Model Explorer for your model format.

(Arm plugin)
VGF adapter

(Arm plugin)

User Guide
and try out major features:
Graph Navigation
Split View Side by Side

Voxtral 3 introduces a cutting-edge voice agent SDK and state-of-the-art speech models designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across 50+ languages. It combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration for seamless workflow automation. Available via Mistral’s EU-hosted API or self-deployment, it ensures data sovereignty while delivering low-latency, human-like interactions for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.
Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult.
A reliable voice agent needs to do four things very well (and simultaneously):
Listen accurately
across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,
Reason
deeply
about what users mean in specific contexts,
Speak naturally
with emotion and expression, and
Take action
over multiple steps through connected systems.
Getting all four to work together reliably in real time remains a challenge.
To address this, we introduce Voxtral 3: a new family of state-of-the-art
speech-to-text
and
text-to-speech
models, alongside a voice agent SDK that brings listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline.
Voxtral 3 is built to create natural conversational experiences, from contact-center agents and service desks to virtual assistants and hands-free copilots. With support for dozens of languages, expressive speech, complex reasoning, and deep integration with your own tools and data, agents built with Voxtral can interpret nuanced intent, reason through sophisticated requests, and execute multi-step actions across connected systems.
As with other Mistral models, the Voxtral 3 family is designed for sovereign deployment. Available today through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment on your own infrastructure, it gives organizations control over where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are retained.

Accurate transcription across 50+ languages

Human-like intelligence at your (spoken) command

Pro Voice for distinctly accurate voice adaptation

Your voice AI, on your infrastructure

Summary
Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.
Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.
Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.
Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)
Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.
Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.
Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.
Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.
Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.
Benchmark Results
We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.
GIFT-Eval - GMean MASE
GIFT-Eval - GMean WQL
GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.
TIME - GMean MASE
TIME - GMean CRPS
TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.
fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.
Family of models optimised for every specification
Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.
Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.
Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.
An industrial example
Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.
Multivariate forecasting.
A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.
Probabilistic forecasting.
A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.
Categorical covariates.
Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.
Known-future covariates.
Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.
From Model to System
Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.
In the plant, that could look like this:
Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.
The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.
Key technical contributions
Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.
Decoupled Horizon Forecasting.
Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
Covariate-aware attention.
Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
Synthetic-first data.
The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
Two-stage training.
Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.
A model that can be adapted
Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.
For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through
Mistral Forge
, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:
Zero-shot inference
out of the box.
Architectural extensions
, such as domain-specific covariates.
Fine-tuning on proprietary data
, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
Control over the training data
, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.
The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.
What’s next
We have published a
GitHub repository
so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

Perplexity Computer now runs fully local on Mac
Perplexity Computer runs fully local on Mac: Work across private files and native apps with AI that stays on your device
Oct 20, 2026
Today, weâre launching
Computer fully local on Mac
, making it possible to run the AI model, harness, and task execution entirely on device. When given permission, Computer can work across local files and Mac apps like Notes and Mail without sending personal data to the cloud. This gives users more control over sensitive data and credit spend.
Each advance in models and hardware expands what AI can accomplish on a personal computer. As more demanding workflows become practical to run locally, the machines people already own will take on a larger share of their AI work.
We first brought Computer to local files and native Mac apps with
Personal Computer
for Mac in May. Last month,
Hybrid Compute
combined frontier reasoning in the cloud with local models that process private information on the Mac, coordinating both parts of the task automatically.
This takes it a step further with the entire task run fully local on Macs with Apple silicon.
More choice in how to complete work
The
Perplexity Mac app
offers two ways to run Computer. Hybrid Compute starts in the cloud, coordinating research and reasoning with local work on private files. Running Computer locally starts on the Mac, keeping the taskâs planning, reasoning, and file processing on device.
Computer uses the Macâs own processing power to complete work locally. It runs Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro, a post-trained version of Qwen. With powerful AI compute available on their Macs, individuals can perform complex, multi-step work while keeping private or sensitive data on their machines.
Running Computer locally, the choice of where to run tasks and how to use credits is completely in the userâs hand. A portfolio analysis based on private holdings and downloaded market data can run entirely on device. A deal review that combines current market research with confidential financials can use Hybrid Compute.
Users can authorize Computer to escalate to the cloud for current information, browser use, and connected apps. The local orchestrator can call on one of 15+ frontier models for advanced reasoning.
Work across Mac files and apps
Running on Mac locally brings Computerâs ability to plan tasks, use tools, and complete multi-step work to the Mac. When users give it permission, Computer works across local files and supported apps, including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers.
Local Computer can read a projectâs to-do list in Notes, check a teammateâs request for a budget update in Messages, and pull planned and actual spending from Excel. It can then prepare a status update showing open tasks and remaining budget, and send a meeting invitation to discuss next steps.
Security and controlled access
With both the model and agent running locally, sensitive work can stay on the Mac through every stage of a task, from planning and analysis to the finished output.
Code and tool execution run in isolated sandbox environments with controlled access to files and connected apps. These same security protocols persist in the cloud version of Perplexity Computer.
Computer works across local workflows
Local Computer can work with private files and information across a range of tasks. Examples include:
Portfolio review
: Computer checks private holdings against investment guidelines and downloaded market data on a Mac mini. It flags concentration risk and allocation drift, then updates an Excel workbook and Keynote deck for the analystâs review.
Client proposal:
Computer turns confidential discovery notes, a client brief, and an internal rate sheet into a proposal. It drafts the scope, builds a budget in Excel, and prepares a cover email in Outlook for review.
Morning priorities
: Computer reviews recent conversations in Messages and Mail, identifies requests and deadlines, and creates an action list in Notes. It gathers relevant local documents and drafts follow-up replies for review.
Available on supported Apple silicon Macs
Local Computer on Mac is now available to Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. It runs in the Perplexity Mac app on supported Apple silicon Macs, like the new Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro. For running Computer locally on Mac, 36 GB or more is recommended. It launches with Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro as local model options.
To get started:
Download and open the latest
Perplexity Mac app
.
Follow the in-app instructions to download and set up a local model.
Choose fully local to run the task on the Mac.

running Computer locally on Mac
today.

Rollouts and Security Review
Today we're launching two Cursor bots for the last mile of shipping code. Rollouts watches every change as it deploys and reports its health per environment. Security Review reports exploitable bugs on every pull request.
Both are available today on Teams and Enterprise plans.
#
Rollouts
Rollouts attaches a monitor to every pull request and watches the change as it deploys, reporting change health per environment: verified healthy, regression detected, or inconclusive. It's the Cursor version of
Firetiger
Change Monitors, rebuilt with the Bot Development Kit.
Enable it from the dashboard and connect source control, your deploy system, and your telemetry provider. Rollouts starts watching on the next pull request.
#
Monitoring plans
When a pull request opens, Rollouts reads the diff and the systems it touches, then writes a monitoring plan as a PR comment. The plan lists the risks it identified, the effect the change is meant to have, the signals it will check, and any gaps in instrumentation that would make the change hard to verify. Edit the plan in the PR and Rollouts uses your version.
#
Deploy tracking
Rollouts wakes on deploy events for the change's commit and runs the plan against your logs, metrics, and traces. It tracks each environment separately, so a change can be verified in staging and still flagged in production. Rollouts checks the change's intended effect alongside error and latency signals, and reports back on the PR when it reaches a verdict.
#
Regressions
When Rollouts detects a regression, it names the change it suspects and notifies the author. Depending on configuration, it can also open a revert PR for review or hand the finding to a cloud agent for a fix. Rollouts does not merge or roll back on its own today.
#
Integrations
Rollouts connects to Origin or GitHub for source control, to your continuous delivery system for deploy events, and to Datadog and other telemetry providers for signals. Feature flag integration is coming soon.
#
Security Review
Security Review is available today. It reads every pull request in the context of the codebase and posts one review comment reporting exploitable bugs. Style and quality stay with Bugbot.
Enable it from the dashboard for the repositories you want reviewed. Draft PRs are skipped.
#
What it reports
Security Review looks for injection across SQL, command, and template surfaces, along with authentication and authorization bypasses, including checks that a refactor stopped running. It also flags secrets and credentials committed to source, SSRF and unvalidated redirects, unsafe deserialization, and dependency changes that introduce known vulnerabilities. It traces where user input enters and what it passes through.
#
Findings
Each finding carries a severity, the attack path, and a proposed fix. Dismiss one with a reason and Security Review won't raise it again on that PR.
#
Team rules
Add rules for your codebase, such as which client external calls must go through or which tables are never queried from a request handler, and Security Review enforces them on every PR.
#
Get started

automations
tab.

Today we're launching Projects in Cursor. Projects lets you take on larger bodies of work, such as a feature, a migration, or a full app. It maintains context over months of work, delegates tasks to thousands of subagents, and performs recurring work without being prompted.
Access Projects from the left-hand nav. The coordinator agent in a project doesn't write code itself; it plans the work, delegates it to agents that implement it, and brings the finished work back to you to check. Coordinators create and manage agents on your behalf, running as many in parallel as the work needs.

Powered by Cloud Agents
A Project runs on its own computer in the cloud, so closing your laptop doesn't stop it. When something needs testing on your machine, the coordinator spins up a local agent to run it there.
#
Shared context
You shouldn't have to onboard an agent every time you start a task. Each Project maintains a set of files that sync across every cloud and local machine its agents use. Agents add research and artifacts, along with what they learn about the codebase and how you prefer work to be done. If one agent figures out how to test a service, for example, every future agent can use those instructions. The shared context grows with the Project, making the coordinator more effective over time.
#
Subscriptions
Tell the coordinator agent to watch a Slack channel, run on a schedule, or follow all your PRs. This way it can take action based on signals it detects, without waiting for your prompt.
Connect Slack and point it at a bug-report channel, and it starts delegating each time a bug comes in.

North 2: Enterprise AI without compromises
North 2 is Cohere’s biggest upgrade yet — unifying enterprise‑grade security, intelligence, cost governance, and full‑stack control into a single agentic AI platform that runs wherever your data lives.
Blog
Written By
Cohere Team
Tags
Product Launch
Share
AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Key takeaways
New agent harness:
North 2 has a redesigned orchestration system enabling more sophisticated, reliable, multi-step automations and agents across the enterprise.
Increased intelligence:
Build smarter workflows and richer agent chat experiences using memory, libraries, skills, artifact, and app creation.
Model agnostic:
Whether you’re using Cohere’s models — or bringing your own — use the models that support your team’s best work.
AI sovereignty:
You’ll get full control over where and how AI runs, with flexible cloud, on‑premises, and air‑gapped deployments.
Enterprise governance:
North admin adds granular cost controls, rate limits, user quotas, and org-wide caps for predictable, governed AI operations.
For the past few years, enterprises have been racing to deploy agentic AI, and they’ve paid for it in complexity, cost, and compromise. Every option demanded a sacrifice: the platform that's secure enough wasn’t smart enough; the one that's smart enough wasn’t controllable enough; the one you could govern became too expensive to run at scale.
North 2
is where that tradeoff ends.
Over the last year, Cohere has rolled out North across high-stakes industries, including finance, healthcare, telecommunications, manufacturing, energy, and the public sector, investing deeply in large-scale production deployments. This has shaped North 2 into a full-stack agentic platform built for organizations that can't afford to compromise on security, intelligence, cost, or control. Enterprises choose North to ensure the journey to AI ROI is more predictable, transparent, and fully owned by the enterprise.
Here's what that looks like in practice.
Intelligence that scales with your enterprise
North works with your knowledge, and now you can teach it more about what success means within your organization.
Users can now create reusable agents and automations that can be shared across the organization, eliminating the need to rebuild similar workflows repeatedly. Prototype documents or apps directly in chat, or connect North to your favorite existing tools.
At the core of North 2 is an advanced agent orchestration system that manages complex, multi-step processes independently. Build agents and automations with simple prompts, and automate your most tedious workflows — helping keep humans-in-the-loop where it matters.
Core features included in North 2
Skills
: Reusable capabilities agents can call on, so no employee wastes time rebuilding the same logic.
Libraries
: Shared knowledge and assets that the whole org can draw from.
Memory
: Agents that keep context across sessions, instead of starting cold every time.
Applications
: Prototype and ship decks, dashboards, documents, and lightweight apps from natural language.
Automations
: Pre-built templates for common processes, a drag-and-drop visual workflow builder, real-time performance monitoring, and integrations with the tools you already use.
Connectors
: Connect North to your data, with new connectors including enterprise connectors to Slack, SharePoint, OneDrive, Microsoft Outlook, Microsoft Exchange, Jira, Linear, Notion, and GitHub, plus planned financial data providers PitchBook, Crunchbase, Daloopa, FiscalAI, S&P Global, FactSet, among others.
LG CNS leverages North to bring AI to customers at scale across South Korea to unlock real business value.
“North gives enterprises a secure, practical foundation for turning agentic AI into real business value. Our experience using North within LG CNS and bringing it to customers across Korea has reinforced our confidence in its ability to scale intelligent automation across the enterprise.”
— Yohan Jin, Head of AI Center, LG CNS
Enterprise-first security
Agentic AI changes the risk calculus for every enterprise security team. With agents that touch internal tools, and models that risk exposure to prompt injection, it has never been more important to safeguard data.
North was built for that reality. It deploys privately on-prem, in the cloud, or fully air-gapped, and North Admin lets teams enforce guardrails at the individual agent level, so rolling agentic AI out to an entire workforce doesn't mean rolling out risk alongside it. Your knowledge graph gets smarter while your knowledge remains safe, never at risk of leaving the premises.
Core features included in North 2
Deployment flexibility:
Select the deployment environment that best suits your security needs (self-hosted, VPC, hybrid, or on-premises).
Exceeding global security standards:
with SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, and ISO 42001 certifications.
Guardrails:
Get guardrails to filter content, improve safety, and validate model responses.
Autonomy policies:
Build agents designed to only take actions they are authorized to take, and seek human oversight for critical decisions or actions.
Rigorous security:
Proactively identify and mitigate potential threats through continual security testing, including red-teaming exercises and third-party vulnerability scanning.
System observability:
Gain visibility into North's operations with easy-to-use tools for monitoring service performance and detailed logs of all changes.
To highlight another example, Bell Cyber is partnering with North to bring government‑grade security to agentic AI.
At Bell Cyber, we see every day how quickly the threat landscape is evolving, and how much security and data sovereignty matter to the organizations we protect. North lets us bring agentic AI into our security operations with the control, privacy, and sovereignty requirements our customers demand built in from the start.
That's important not only for strengthening how we defend Bell and our customers, but for helping Canadian businesses and governments adopt agentic AI securely and with confidence.
— Jawed Ahmad, Chief Technology and AI Officer, Bell Cyber
Granular controls, improved tokenomics
North Admin delivers enterprise-grade controls. Admins set roles and permissions, and control which models get used where and by who. Additionally, admins can monitor and manage activity in real time with detailed analytics, and get granular details or see a systems-level overview of AI investment usage, including token spend and limits.
Before limits are set, thresholds for alerts can notify teams of risk. Whether your organization measures adoption or model consumption, Cohere provides the tooling to measure AI ROI.
Core features included in North 2
North Admin:
Configure visibility to your desired level, including down to the user and agent level, so enterprises know exactly how their AI is being used, and can guardrail it accordingly.
Granular access controls and permissions:
Integrate with your existing identity and access management systems, and get enhanced authentication and granular admin controls.
Flow control:
Monitor and control token spend and limiting by defining consumption tiers based on requests and token rates for users and groups.
Efficient token consumption:
When using NVIDIA hardware with Cohere models, get increased tokens per second per node, effectively decreasing spend.
Bring your organization’s existing models:
North is model agnostic, use our generative model offerings or bring your favorites.
Additionally, our collaboration with
NVIDIA
finds that North generates more insights, for fewer tokens, with Cohere models trained and deployed on
NVIDIA Blackwell
and Hopper. That means fewer spent tokens, without sacrificing model intelligence. See more on our models
here
.
Organizations need control over where their AI runs and how their data is secured,” said Kari Briski, Vice President of Generative AI at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA Blackwell and Hopper accelerate inference for Cohere models, helping North 2.0 deliver more tokens for less.
Find your organization’s true North
For organizations that demand rigor in their AI investments, North 2 leads with production-ready, full-stack AI solutions. With North, get end-to-end, customizable, capable, and secure tooling that integrates with existing systems and helps protect sensitive data — that point teams on the path to true AI for empowerment.
North was built to be owned, and it is increasingly built to be specialized. With North, even the most regulated industries can adopt agentic AI confidently, knowing their deployments align with their operational, compliance, and governance needs.

Introducing North Small Translate: A leading sovereign open-weight machine translation model
Outsized performance, right-sized footprint — translation built for speed and cost efficiency.
Blog
Written By
Cohere Team
Tags
Product Launch
Share
AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Today, we're releasing North Small Translate, a mixture-of-experts machine translation model with strong performance across 50+ languages. Across WMT26 benchmarks,¹ North Small Translate achieves an 83.6 score across all languages, outperforming proprietary models like DeepL and Google Translate, as well as open-weight alternatives such as Gemma 4 31B (off), GLM 5.2, and Mistral Large 3.
North Small Translate marks a significant milestone as Cohere's first translation model in the North model family. It builds on our multilingual and translation lineage — from the
Tiny Aya model family
to
Command A Translate
— and represents a clear next step in Cohere’s commitment to offering high-quality machine translation wherever it is needed.
Now available for research and non-commercial use under a
CC BY-NC 4.0
license, North Small Translate advances Cohere’s mission to make sovereign AI a technological reality.
Visit
Hugging Face
to download the weights - available in several near-lossless quantizations - explore our
HuggingFace space
to demo the model, and read our
implementation guides
.
